## Research findings

The claim that Czechoslovakia retained a larger Jewish population than most other Nazi-occupied countries is false both in absolute numbers and in survival rate. Prewar Czechoslovakia had 356,830 Jews by religion in the 1930 census: 117,551 in Bohemia and Moravia, 136,737 in Slovakia, and 102,542 in Subcarpathian Rus https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-holocaust-in-bohemia-and-moravia . Germans and collaborators killed approximately 263,000 Jews who had resided in 1938 Czechoslovak territory https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-holocaust-in-bohemia-and-moravia . For the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia specifically, of 82,309 Jews deported, about 71,000 were killed, plus another 7,000 killed in Bohemia and Moravia, leaving by 1945 some 14,000 Protectorate Jews alive in the Czech lands https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-holocaust-in-bohemia-and-moravia . Comparative survival was much higher elsewhere: in Western Europe around three-quarters of prewar Jews survived in France and Italy, about half survived in Belgium, while only a quarter survived in the Netherlands; in eastern/south-eastern Europe most Bulgarian Jews survived, as well as 60% in Romania and nearly 30% in Hungary, two-thirds survived in the Soviet Union, whereas Bohemia, Slovakia and Yugoslavia lost about 80% and Poland, the Baltic states and Greece lost close to 90% https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors . In absolute terms, prewar populations were Poland ~3,000,000, Soviet Union European part 2,525,000, Romania 756,000, Germany ~525,000, Hungary 445,000, Czechoslovakia 357,000, France 250,000, Netherlands 156,000 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-population-of-europe-in-1933-population-data-by-country , so even with high murder rates Poland still had ~300,000 flight survivors alone who fled to Soviet-occupied Poland/interior https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors , far exceeding ~14,000 in Czech lands plus limited Slovak survivors. France with ~75% survival of 250,000 (~180,000+ survivors), Romania with ~60% of 756,000 (~450,000 survivors), Hungary with ~30% of 445,000 (~130,000 survivors) all dwarf Czechoslovak remainder. The accompanying rationale about Nazis sparing Jewish doctors for medical care is also contrary to evidence that Protectorate Jews including doctors were systematically deported via Theresienstadt to killing sites with few survivors https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-holocaust-in-bohemia-and-moravia .

- The property was mostly financed by a loan from Jaan Tallinn's company, not by FTX money. - The deposits were sent in July and August 2022, months before FTX collapsed in November 2022. That does not fit the phrase 'as it was collapsing'. David Morris's excerpt does describe a flood of payments in the weeks before the collapse as an attempt to move money out, but it ties the property deposits to July and August (https://davidzmorris.substack.com/p/a-lever-long-enough-draft-excerpt).

- These are allegations in a civil clawback suit, not established findings. A Community Note on the article says Lightcone's CEO disputes that FTX money was used for the purchase (https://commonnotes.net/).

**Recipient.** According to the same complaint, the $1M went to a title company as an escrow deposit, not to CFAR. SFGate reports the same deposit: https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php. The complaint says the transfers were meant as a loan. His work is cited in Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig's undergraduate textbook Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach on Friendly AI and mechanism design https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliezer_Yudkowsky . Other bios describe him as "decision theorist, computer scientist, and author who co-founded and leads research at MIRI" and as "researcher, writer, and philosopher on superintelligent AI". He lacks formal credentials — "autodidact" who "did not attend high school or college" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliezer_Yudkowsky — which critics use to deny scientist status, but in functional terms he has worked 20+ years as a full-time AI safety / decision-theory researcher, so claiming he is "not a scientist of any kind" is false by common usage of researcher / computer scientist.

Markets are highly skewed/non-linear: 67% of users are men vs 33% women, men average 15,609 right swipes vs 2,283 for women, yet women's average match rate 44.4% vs men's 5.26% (median 41.27% vs 2.04%), women reject ~95% of profiles https://github.com/boe-ventures/swipestats.io/blob/HEAD/content/posts/dating-app-statistics-gender.mdx . Same data notes vicious cycle where men's volume strategy leads algorithm to depress visibility and women's match quality falls, so "men who carpet-bomb actually get worse results than they would with selective swiping" https://github.com/boe-ventures/swipestats.io/blob/HEAD/content/posts/dating-app-statistics-gender.mdx . Lowering standards monotonically expands eligible pool but pool size follows cumulative attractiveness/selectivity distributions and other-side selectivity, not a constant linear slope, and comes with quality/cost tradeoffs. Approximate linearity only holds if acceptance probability p is constant (expected dates = n*p), which evidence above shows is false in selective, imbalanced, algorithm-mediated markets.

samples.research:
The tweet claims Steam itself enforces DRM that requires re-authentication every 30 days, and that all games would break permanently if Steam's servers went down. This significantly overstates and mischaracterizes how Steam's systems actually work.

A Valve developer (Henry Goffin) explicitly stated on Steam's own forums that '"Offline Mode is designed to be indefinite"' and that 'the client should allow you to run in Offline Mode for as long as you like' (https://www.pcgamesn.com/steam-offline-mode-designed-be-indefinite-valve-are-working-make-it-more-robust, https://kotaku.com/valve-is-constantly-trying-to-improve-steams-wonky-o-1458484605). Valve clarified that the periodic 'two-week' or '30-day' check-in some users experienced was actually a bug, not an intentional design/DRM policy — Valve's post states it 'is not broken by design' and that the timeout issue 'has been fixed for months now' (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/1/864969953572102601).

Separately, Steam community discussion confirms that the ~30-day re-authentication requirement that does exist for some games comes from third-party DRM systems (e.g., Denuvo, Ubisoft Connect, Battle.net) bundled by individual publishers/developers, not from Steam's own universal DRM: 'If you have games with Denuvo or other DRM, of launchers, they will ask to phone home every period (like 30 days)' and 'Offline mode doesn't have any kind of automatic expiration. You can use Steam in offline mode forever' (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/587308261888419215/). Another thread states the 2-week authentication expiration 'only matters for games that use server-side Steam DRM (e.g. Denuvo)' and 'this 2 week limitation used to apply to all games on Steam, but was patched out of Steam's client-side DRM in ~2013' (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/2798376078346605932).

This directly supports the position of the quoted post that Steam itself does not require DRM and that any re-authentication requirements are a developer/publisher decision via third-party DRM, not an inherent Steam-enforced DRM policy. In the UK, MoneyNerd explains 'A write-off can be requested, but illness does not automatically cancel every debt' and 'Reasonable adjustments... do not create a general right to have the debt cancelled or its financial terms rewritten' https://moneynerd.co.uk/write-off-debt-illness/ . My Debt Plan explains write-off due to mental health is only 'In certain circumstances, it is possible to ask creditors to write off your debts' as 'a last resort, typically when your situation is unlikely to improve, and there are no assets or income to pay the debt' and 'Creditors are not obligated to agree' https://mydebt-plan.co.uk/debt-management/debt-and-mental-health/ . In US contract-law context, Get Out of Debt Guy explains debts signed while impaired/medicated are generally 'voidable, not automatically void' and 'the law does not erase it on its own; you have to challenge it' and hospitalization/incapacity 'does not wipe out the debt' https://getoutofdebt.org/269757/signed-debt-while-medicated-pressured-do-i-still-owe-it . No South Africa source supports automatic cancellation; SA consumer debt is dealt with via application-based debt review under the National Credit Act and sequestration/administration under the Insolvency Act, not by hospital admission alone. The claim reverses a discretionary, creditor-by-creditor hardship request into a guaranteed universal cancellation, which is false and could encourage self-harm/hospitalization for financial reasons.

The claim in the post is a widely circulated piece of internet folklore about cornrows being used by slaves to create escape maps and hide food/seeds. Snopes investigated this story twice (2022 and again in May 2026, coinciding closely with this tweet's posting date) and found it to be unverified legend rather than confirmed history. Truthorfiction.com similarly concluded 'Historians remain divided on the authenticity of such claims; their popularity persists' (https://www.truthorfiction.com/did-slaves-braid-routes-to-freedom-into-hairstyles/), comparing it to the similarly unverified 'quilt code' Underground Railroad legend.

Wikipedia's entry on Biohó notes this is largely folkloric: 'while there is no direct relationship between him and the municipality of San Basilio de Palenque, contemporary literary culture has led to the belief that he was the founder of the town, though this is inaccurate' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benkos_Bioh%C3%B3). The Wikipedia Cornrows article itself frames this as folklore, not fact: 'According to Black folklore, cornrows were often used to communicate on the Underground Railroad and by Benkos Biohó during his time as a slave in Colombia' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornrows).

Support for the claim mostly rests on oral history from Afro-Colombian communities (e.g., a 2011 Washington Post feature on hair braider Ziomara Asprilla Garcia) and one academic paper based on tour-guide testimony at Elmina Castle in Ghana, not on direct historical/archival evidence from the era of American slavery. The Ancient Origins article notes 'it's hard to say since official history has usually been told by white men and a form of resistance amongst the African diaspora by definition lacks archival evidence' (https://www.ancient-origins.net/weird-facts/braids-0017595).

In short, this is a popular but historically unverified legend — not a confirmed fact — that fact-checkers have been unable to substantiate with primary historical evidence, particularly regarding American slavery specifically.

samples.research: The claim in the tweet—that cornrows were used by runaway slaves to map escape routes and store food (seeds/rice) for their journey—is a widely circulated internet legend without solid historical verification. Snopes investigated this claim twice (2022 and again in 2026) and found no tangible evidence it occurred among enslaved people in the U.S. Their 2026 fact-check states: "We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages" (https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). Snopes classifies this as a 'Legend'—a story 'so general or lacking in detail they could have happened to someone, somewhere, at some time, and are therefore essentially unprovable' (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check-ratings/). The documented version of this story is specific to Colombia, tied to Benkos Bioho and the Palenque community in the 17th century, not to U.S. slavery broadly as the tweet implies—Snopes notes 'It is most documented in Colombia where Benkos Bioho, a king captured from Africa by the Portuguese who escaped slavery, built San Basillio de Palenque' (https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). Even in the Colombian context, experts caution this is an oral-history legend rather than verified history, comparing it to the debunked myth of coded quilts on the Underground Railroad: 'historians have been interrogating the myth of messages in quilts for a while. Numerous experts argued that such ideas were too fanciful a construction' (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/). The 'rice/seeds hidden in hair' claim similarly traces to oral histories and legends among Suriname Maroon descendants recorded by researchers like Judith Carney, not direct documentary evidence—Snopes notes 'the presence of the crop is attributed to female ancestors' hiding rice in their hair as they fled sugar plantations to freedom' as a legend recounted by descendants (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/). Critics online have also raised practical objections, arguing it is implausible that enough rice/seeds could be hidden in hair to sustain someone, or that seeds would survive sweat and time without rotting, as discussed in a forum thread (https://www.lipstickalley.com/threads/slaves-used-cornrows-to-transfer-and-create-maps-to-leave-plantations.4570251/). In short, this is a popular but historically unverified legend lacking primary-source documentation, often presented as established fact on social media when professional fact-checkers have been unable to substantiate it.
